objectives.text: Know the SI base quantities and units (mass, length, time, current, temperature, amount of substance) and express derived units in base units.
Use SI prefixes from pico to tera and convert between units sensibly.
Check whether an equation is homogeneous using base units.
Distinguish random from systematic errors, and precision/repeatability from accuracy.
Assess uncertainties in measurements and calculated results, as absolute, fractional and percentage values.
Combine uncertainties for sums, differences, products, quotients and powers.
Distinguish scalars from vectors, and add, subtract and resolve vectors into components.
Define and use displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
Interpret displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, using gradients and areas.
Derive and use the constant-acceleration equations such as $v = u + at$ and $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$.
Analyse free fall and the acceleration of free fall $g$, including experimental determination.
Treat projectile motion by resolving it into independent horizontal and vertical components.
State and apply Newton's three laws of motion.
Define mass, weight, and linear momentum, and relate force to rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p/\Delta t$.
Explain free-fall and terminal velocity effects of drag and viscous forces.
Apply conservation of momentum in one and two dimensions to collisions and explosions.
Distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions using kinetic energy.
Relate impulse to force-time graphs and change in momentum.
Describe the nature and origin of gravitational, electric, magnetic, upthrust, friction, drag and tension forces, and draw free-body diagrams.
Define and use density, $\rho = m/V$.
Define and use pressure, $p = F/A$, and hydrostatic pressure $p = \rho g h$.
Explain the origin of upthrust and use $F = \rho g V$.
Define the moment of a force, torque of a couple, and apply the principle of moments.
Use equilibrium conditions: no resultant force and no resultant moment, including triangle of forces.
Define and use work done by a force, including $W = Fs\cos\theta$ and $W = p\Delta V$.
Distinguish gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, using $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ and $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$.
Apply conservation of energy to mechanical situations and recognise energy dissipation.
Define and use power, $P = W/t$ and $P = Fv$.
Calculate efficiency as useful output over total input.
Describe how tensile and compressive forces deform a material.
Define and use Hooke's law, the spring constant and elastic limit, $F = kx$.
Define stress, strain and the Young modulus, and determine the Young modulus experimentally.
Use force-extension graphs to find the work done and the elastic potential energy $E = \tfrac12 Fx$.
Distinguish elastic from plastic deformation and describe ductile, brittle and polymeric behaviour from stress-strain curves.
Describe progressive waves and define displacement, amplitude, wavelength, period, frequency, phase difference and wave speed.
Use $v = f\lambda$ and relate intensity to amplitude, $I \propto A^2$, and to power per unit area.
Distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves and describe polarisation and Malus-type intensity changes.
Describe the electromagnetic spectrum, its regions and their approximate wavelengths, and that all waves travel at $c$ in a vacuum.
Use the Doppler effect for sound, $f_o = f_s v/(v \pm v_s)$.
Interpret graphs of wave displacement against distance and time.
Apply the principle of superposition and explain stationary waves, nodes and antinodes.
Describe stationary waves on strings and in air columns, and determine wavelength and speed from them.
Explain diffraction at a single slit and its dependence on slit width and wavelength.
Explain interference and the conditions for coherence, including two-source interference and Young's double slit, $\lambda = ax/D$.
Use the diffraction grating equation $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$.
Define electric current, charge and the elementary charge, with $Q = It$.
Define potential difference, electromotive force, and relate energy to charge, $V = W/Q$.
Use $I = nAvq$ to describe current in terms of charge carriers.
Define resistance and resistivity, $R = \rho L/A$, and use $V = IR$.
Sketch and interpret I-V characteristics of resistors, filament lamps, diodes and thermistors.
Calculate electrical power, $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$, and energy transferred.
Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using standard symbols.
Apply Kirchhoff's first law (conservation of charge) and second law (conservation of energy).
Calculate the combined resistance of resistors in series and in parallel.
Explain internal resistance and its effect on terminal potential difference.
Analyse potential dividers, including with thermistors and LDRs.
Explain the use of potentiometer circuits for comparing potential differences.
Describe the nuclear atom model and the evidence from alpha-particle scattering.
Describe the proton, neutron and electron composition of the nucleus and use nucleon and proton numbers for isotopes.
Apply conservation of charge, nucleon number and mass-energy in nuclear equations.
Describe alpha, beta and gamma decay and the resulting changes in the nucleus.
Describe the quark model: up, down and strange quarks, and hadrons as made of quarks.
Classify leptons and hadrons, and explain beta decay in terms of quark change and the neutrino.
Define the radian and convert between radians and degrees.
Define angular velocity and use $v = r\omega$ and $\omega = 2\pi/T$.
Explain that circular motion requires a centripetal force towards the centre.
Use $a = v^2/r = r\omega^2$ and $F = mv^2/r = mr\omega^2$ for circular motion problems.
Describe a gravitational field as a region where mass experiences a force and define gravitational field strength.
Use Newton's law of gravitation, $F = GMm/r^2$, for point masses.
Derive and use $g = GM/r^2$ for the field of a point mass and recognise its uniformity near the surface.
Define gravitational potential and use $\phi = -GM/r$, with potential energy changes.
Analyse circular orbits, derive Kepler's third law, and describe geostationary orbits.
Use escape-related ideas via the area under a field strength-distance graph.
Explain thermal equilibrium and the zero-law basis for temperature measurement.
Convert between the Celsius and thermodynamic (Kelvin) scales and describe absolute zero.
Explain how physical properties are used in thermometers and compare their sensitivity and range.
Define and use specific heat capacity and specific latent heats of fusion and vaporisation.
Describe how to determine specific heat capacity and latent heat experimentally.
Use the equation of state $pV = nRT$ and $pV = NkT$, with the mole and Avogadro constant.
State the assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.
Derive and use $pV = \tfrac13 Nm\langle c^2\rangle$ for gas pressure.
Show that mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\tfrac32 kT$ and use it with r.m.s. speed.
Explain Boyle's law and the pressure and temperature laws from kinetic theory.
Explain internal energy as the sum of random kinetic and potential energies of molecules.
Relate internal energy changes to temperature and phase changes.
Apply the first law, $\Delta U = q + w$, with sign conventions.
Calculate work done by or on a gas at constant pressure, $w = p\Delta V$, and interpret p-V diagrams.
Describe free, damped and forced oscillations and define amplitude, period, frequency and angular frequency.
Define simple harmonic motion, $a = -\omega^2 x$, and use displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs.
Use $x = x_0\sin\omega t$, $v = \pm\omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x^2}$ and $v_0 = \omega x_0$.
Analyse energy exchange in SHM between kinetic and potential forms.
Describe light, critical and heavy damping, with practical examples.
Explain resonance in forced oscillations and the effect of damping on the amplitude-frequency curve.
Describe an electric field as a region where a charge feels a force, and define field strength $E = F/q$.
Use Coulomb's law, $F = Qq/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2)$, and the field of a point charge.
Use $E = V/d$ for a uniform field and describe motion of charged particles in it.
Define electric potential and use $V = Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$ with potential energy.
Relate field strength to potential gradient and interpret field and potential graphs.
Draw and interpret field lines and equipotentials.
Define capacitance, $C = Q/V$, and use series and parallel combinations.
Determine energy stored in a capacitor, $W = \tfrac12 QV = \tfrac12 CV^2$, from a charge-voltage graph.
Analyse capacitor charging and discharging through a resistor, using the time constant $\tau = RC$.
Use exponential discharge relations such as $x = x_0 e^{-t/RC}$ for charge, current and voltage.
Describe magnetic fields from currents and magnets, including field lines for wires, coils and solenoids.
Use the force on a current-carrying conductor, $F = BIL\sin\theta$, and define the tesla.
Use $F = Bqv\sin\theta$ and analyse charged particle paths in magnetic and electric fields, including velocity selectors.
Explain the Hall effect and use the Hall probe to measure flux density.
Define magnetic flux and flux linkage, $\Phi = BA$.
State and apply Faraday's and Lenz's laws to induced e.m.f.
Explain induced e.m.f. in moving conductors, generators and transformers (including losses).
Describe sinusoidal alternating current and voltage, with peak value, period and frequency.
Relate r.m.s. values to peak values, $I_{rms} = I_0/\sqrt2$, and calculate mean power.
Explain half-wave and full-wave rectification with diodes, and smoothing with a capacitor.
Describe the photon model and calculate photon energy, $E = hf$.
Explain the photoelectric effect and its evidence for the particle nature of light.
Use $hf = \phi + E_{k,max}$ and the threshold frequency and work function.
Describe electron diffraction as evidence for wave-particle duality and use $\lambda = h/p$.
Explain line emission and absorption spectra using discrete energy levels, $hf = E_2 - E_1$.
Describe X-ray production and the continuous and characteristic spectra.
Explain atomic energy levels and the relation to spectral lines.
Explain mass defect and binding energy, and use $E = mc^2$.
Interpret the binding energy per nucleon curve and explain fusion and fission energy release.
Describe radioactive decay as random and spontaneous and define activity and decay constant.
Use $A = \lambda N$ and $x = x_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ for activity and number of nuclei.
Define half-life and use $\lambda = \ln 2/t_{1/2}$.
Explain the different ionising and penetrating properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
Describe the production and properties of ultrasound and its generation by piezoelectric transducers.
Explain how ultrasound scans use reflection and acoustic impedance, $Z = \rho c$, with intensity reflection coefficients.
Describe the production of X-rays and their attenuation, $I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}$.
Explain how CT scanners build images from X-ray attenuation.
Describe the use of radioactive tracers in PET scanning and the role of annihilation.
Describe MRI imaging principles using magnetic fields, nuclear resonance and radio-frequency pulses.
Explain standard candles and luminosity, and use the inverse square law for radiant flux, $F = L/(4\pi d^2)$.
Describe Wien's displacement law and Stefan-Boltzmann law, $L = 4\pi r^2\sigma T^4$.
Explain how stellar properties are determined from spectra and luminosity.
Use redshift, $\Delta\lambda/\lambda \approx v/c$, to infer recession speed.
State and use Hubble's law, $v = H_0 d$, and relate it to the expansion of the universe and the Big Bang.
Describe the evidence for the Big Bang, including cosmic microwave background radiation, and discuss dark matter and dark energy.
Describe the stages in the life cycle of stars and the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
